core_obligations: Reduction to one presheaf (proof lines 11348-11363): the last statement about being the finest topology is immediate once the family of sieves is a topology, and the family defined by the whole collection is the intersection of the families defined by the individual presheaves, so by the companion result on intersections it suffices to treat a single presheaf.

The axioms for one presheaf (proof lines 11366-11413): the first and third axioms are verified immediately, and the second is proved by reducing along a covering sieve, using the bijectivity defining the family and the sheaf-theoretic manipulations displayed in the text.

The closing verification (proof lines 11411-11412): the author leaves to the reader the verification that the constructed map is inverse to the natural map displayed above, which is the last step of the second axiom.
proof_roadmap: Reduce to a single presheaf by writing the family of sieves as an intersection of families.
Verify the three axioms of a topology for a single presheaf, writing out the second.
Record that the topology obtained is the finest one making the given presheaves into sheaves.
difficulty_reason: The lemma defines, for a collection of presheaves of sets, the family of sieves whose morphism sets are unchanged after restricting along the morphism, and proves that this family is a topology, indeed the finest topology in which all the given presheaves are sheaves (statement lines 11330-11345). The proof is a complete argument: the family is written as an intersection of the families attached to the single presheaves, so the companion result on intersections reduces the statement to one presheaf (proof lines 11348-11363); the three axioms are then verified, the second one in detail by reduction along a covering sieve and sheaf-theoretic manipulations (proof lines 11366-11410); and the author leaves to the reader only the routine check that the constructed map is inverse to the displayed one (proof lines 11411-11412). The non-formal content is the verification of the second axiom. The claim is H2: a reduction followed by an axiom check.
